summary: Provides a framework for loop-free convergence. It explains the causes and consequences of micro-loops, which are transient forwarding loops among routers that occur while the network recomputes routes, and helps readers decide whether they matter. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a network changes, routers may briefly disagree about where to send packets. This RFC explains the resulting micro-loops and compares ways to reduce or prevent them.

questions: what is a micro-loop in routing
how to prevent transient loops during convergence
subtitle: A survey of transient routing loops and approaches for reducing or preventing them.

tldr.problem: During a topology change, routers update their forwarding tables at different times, which can cause packets to loop temporarily.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains when micro-loops occur and surveys mitigation, prevention, suppression, and network-design approaches.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework and survey, not a protocol or a recommendation of one universal solution.

facts.label: Maximum traffic increase on a link

today: RFC 5715 is an Informational framework from January 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It surveys loop-control proposals and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: How Micro-Loops Form
sections.content:
A micro-loop is a temporary packet-forwarding loop among routers. It can occur while routers learn about a topology change, calculate new paths, and update their forwarding information bases at different times.

Loops can form between two routers or around a longer cycle. A looping packet consumes bandwidth until it escapes or its time to live expires, and inconsistent routes can prevent traffic from reaching a fast-reroute repair.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers may learn about a change at different times and briefly send packets to one another in a loop. Those packets use bandwidth and may keep a repair path from receiving traffic.

sections.title: Causes and Consequences
sections.content:
Micro-loops can occur during the reconvergence that follows a topology change. Cyclic loops may form with asymmetric link costs, different choices among equal-cost paths, or changes that affect multiple links.

Looping packets can increase traffic on a link by as much as 128 times and reduce bandwidth available to other traffic. Inconsistent forwarding tables can also prevent packets from reaching a fast-reroute repair, leaving that repair without traffic to protect.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers may disagree about a route when costs or links change. Packets can circulate, crowd links, and fail to reach a backup path.

sections.title: When Loop Control May Be Needed
sections.content:
Micro-loops may follow component failures or repairs, management changes, link-cost changes, external-cost changes, or shared-risk failures. The framework applies to IP networks and MPLS networks using LDP.

Whether a network needs loop control depends on its topology and how quickly its interior gateway protocol converges. The RFC groups approaches into mitigation, prevention, suppression, and network design to reduce the chance of loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Many kinds of network changes can cause micro-loops. Operators should consider both how likely the topology is to loop and how long the routing change takes.

sections.title: Mitigation with PLSN
sections.content:
Faster convergence can reduce how long micro-loops last. The RFC also describes Path Locking with Safe-Neighbors (PLSN), which classifies destinations by whether a router can safely change their next hop.

Some destinations can move immediately; others wait until routers have made earlier safe changes. Simulations described in the RFC show fewer links subject to looping, but PLSN is only a partial solution and loops may still form between certain routers.
sections.plainLanguage: Path Locking with Safe-Neighbors (PLSN) lets routers change routes that are known to be safe and delay harder changes. It can reduce loops, but does not eliminate them in every case.

sections.title: Eight Proposed Prevention Methods
sections.content:
The RFC surveys eight proposals: incremental cost advertisement, nearside tunnels, farside tunnels, distributed tunnels, packet marking, new MPLS labels, ordered forwarding-table updates, and synchronized forwarding-table updates.

These methods make different trade-offs. Some need router cooperation or tunneling support; others add delay, require additional forwarding state, or depend on synchronization. The RFC does not select one method for every network.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposals control when routes change or carry affected packets along temporary paths. Each has requirements and costs that depend on the network.

sections.title: Suppression, Compatibility, and Security
sections.content:
Loop suppression aims to detect looping packets and discard them, limiting their effect on other traffic rather than delivering those packets successfully. The RFC also discusses how methods interact with routers that do not support loop control.

The document is a survey of proposals rather than a deployment specification. It leaves a complete security analysis to the specification of any solution selected for use.
sections.plainLanguage: Some approaches stop a looping packet from harming other traffic instead of finding a route for it. Any chosen solution needs to consider compatibility and its own security.
